episode_title: 110 | How Nate’s Nectar Turned Honey Into a National Brand | Ft. Nathan and Erika Davis

real_qa.q: How did Nathan Davis discover beekeeping and transition from grain farming to starting Nate's Nectar?
real_qa.r: Nathan initially worked on his family's grain farm but went to college for environmental science with a biology minor. During his third year, he interned with the Central Ohio Beekeepers Association (COBA) and found beekeeping fascinating as a different side of agriculture. He then convinced his parents to let him return to the farm and start with four bee packages, which grew to 12 or 16 within the first month due to his fascination with the hives.
real_qa.requete: Nathan Davis Nate's Nectar beekeeping start

real_qa.q: What product innovation did Nate's Nectar introduce after visiting Paris that set them apart from other honey sellers?
real_qa.r: During a research and development trip to Paris, Nathan and Erika discovered creamed honey in Parisian bakeries. They decided to come home and figure out how to make it themselves because they didn't see creamed honey anywhere in the US market. This became their key differentiator from other honey sellers, and they initially made it in a co-op kitchen in North Ohio before building their own FDA kitchen.
real_qa.requete: Nate's Nectar creamed honey Paris discovery

real_qa.q: How did Nate's Nectar switch from extract-based to organic freeze-dried fruit powders in their creamed honey?
real_qa.r: Initially, Nate's Nectar used extracts in their creamed honey because they were easy to mix and shelf-stable. However, through farmer's market feedback, they made a conscious shift to organic freeze-dried fruit powders. This was a huge game changer because the fruit powders produced vibrant colors—like deep blueberry—that made the product pop on retail shelves compared to the uniform creamy color of extract-based versions.
real_qa.requete: Nate's Nectar freeze-dried fruit powders ingredients

real_qa.q: How did Nate's Nectar secure distribution in Giant Eagle Market District stores after starting with grassroots sales?
real_qa.r: In 2019, Erika conducted grassroots outreach in Columbus and Dayton by Googling specialty shops, making a route, and personally walking into stores with samples and sell sheets. On their final stop—an unplanned visit to Giant Eagle Market District—she met the general manager who connected her with eight buyers standing in a semicircle. They were so excited about the product that Nathan had to bring all remaining inventory from the car, and a buyer named David became their main contact for that partnership.
real_qa.requete: Nate's Nectar Giant Eagle Market District retail

real_qa.q: What role do Nathan and Erika's family members play in scaling Nate's Nectar operations?
real_qa.r: Nathan's sister Marissa serves as the COO of Nate's Nectar and runs day-to-day operations including batch mixing. His other sister Lauren handles all graphic design and photography for labels from the beginning. His parents and sisters help with order packing and supply cost optimization. Nathan's mom Emily, along with Marissa and Lauren, ensure every order is packed to the highest standard and proactively identify ways to save on packaging materials.
real_qa.requete: Nate's Nectar family business operations sisters

guest.entreprise_secondaire: Family grain farm, Western Lone County
guest.bio_context: Nathan Davis grew up on his family's grain farm spanning a couple thousand acres in Western Lone County. He studied environmental science with a biology minor and interned with the Central Ohio Beekeepers Association (COBA) during college. After initially pursuing biochemistry, he returned to the farm and started with four bee packages, expanding to 12 or 16 within the first month, eventually building Nate's Nectar into a nationally distributed brand with his wife Erika.
